overview.title: Human Poverty Index
overview.definition: The Human Poverty Index (HPI) is a composite index introduced by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in 1997 in its Human Development Report to measure the deprivation in the basic dimensions of human development in developing (HPI-1) and developed (HPI-2) countries.
overview.importanceInUpsc: Crucial microtopic under UPSC GS Paper III (Economy - Inclusive Growth, Poverty, Human Development) and GS Paper I (Social Issues). Essential for understanding alternative paradigms of poverty measurement beyond mere income deprivation.
learningOutcomes: Master foundational concepts and mechanisms of Human Poverty Index.
Evaluate spatial distribution, institutional frameworks, and policy dimensions.
Apply high-yield mnemonics to solve tricky Prelims and Mains questions.
prerequisites: Basic concepts of Human Development Index (HDI)

sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Multidimensional Paradigm**: HPI shifts focus from income poverty (headcount ratio based on consumption expenditure) to deprivation in basic human capabilities.
• **Introduction Year**: First formulated and published in the **1997 Human Development Report** by the UNDP.
• **Two Variants**: Divided into **HPI-1** (for developing countries) and **HPI-2** (for select high-income OECD countries).
• **Supersession Note**: HPI was succeeded by the **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)** in 2010, developed by the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) and UNDP.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Applied to low- and middle-income nations across Global South including India.

Measures deprivation in survival (probability at birth not surviving to age 40), knowledge (adult illiteracy rate), and economic provisioning (percentage of people without access to safe water and underweight children under 5).
Direct questions on indicators used in early UNDP reports; baseline for evolution into MPI.

Measures deprivation in survival (probability of not surviving to age 60), knowledge (functional illiteracy skills), decent standard of living (percentage living below poverty line, defined as 50% of median disposable household income), and social exclusion (long-term unemployment).
Highlights relative poverty and structural exclusion in advanced economies.
Replaced HPI globally to provide a micro-level, household-based index.
Utilizes 10 indicators across Health, Education, and Standard of Living with equal weighting using Alkire-Foster methodology.
Crucial for current affairs; India's National MPI published by NITI Aayog is based on this methodology.

items.definition: Amartya Sen's capability approach forming the philosophical backbone of HPI, focusing on what individuals are effectively able to do or be.
A mathematical technique used for measuring multidimensional poverty by counting the deprivations each person experiences simultaneously.
The institutional body responsible for conceptualizing, calculating, and publishing global human development and poverty indices.
India's official official multidimensional poverty measure tracking progress across 12 indicators aligned with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Global Concentration**: Highest HPI-1 scores historically concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia due to structural deficits in health and sanitation.
• **Intra-Country Disparities**: Sub-national variations in India showed high poverty incidence in central and eastern states (Bihar, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh) under older deprivation metrics.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Data lag, difficulty in capturing intra-household inequality, and shifting definitions of basic needs over time.
• **Policy Interventions**: Targeted social safety nets (Poshan Abhiyaan, Jal Jeevan Mission, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan) directly addressing erstwhile HPI/MPI deprivations.

items.title: Mnemonic for HPI-1 Dimensions
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "K-S-L" (Knowledge, Survival, Living Standard)
• **Decoded Meaning**: Knowledge (Illiteracy), Survival (Probability of dying before 40), Living standard (Water + Underweight).
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly eliminates options that include income or per capita GDP inside HPI-1.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: HPI measures *deprivation* (what is lacking), whereas HDI measures *achievement* (what is attained), both using parallel dimensions.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that 'HPI includes per capita income or GDP as a direct indicator.' This is completely false. HPI explicitly excludes income, relying instead on non-income deprivations in health, education, and basic living conditions.

Mains Value Addition: Quote Amartya Sen's 'Poverty as Capability Deprivation' framework in GS Paper III answers on inclusive growth. Contrast the income-based poverty line (like Tendulkar or Rangarajan committees) with the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) to showcase analytical depth.

keyTakeaways: HPI was a pioneering composite index created by UNDP in 1997 to measure human deprivation rather than mere financial poverty.
HPI-1 focused on developing nations via metrics of survival, knowledge, and economic provisioning, while HPI-2 targeted OECD nations.
HPI was formally replaced in 2010 by the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), which serves as the foundation for modern poverty tracking, including India's National MPI by NITI Aayog.
